subject: testing for significant differences in species distribution predictions

messages.author: 8156fdd09adbc581
messages.subject: testing for significant differences in species distribution predictions
parts:
Hello,
I followed the vignette on "mapping species distributions" to create maps of big cat occupancy across a landscape over 3 time periods.  I would like to determine if occupancy has changed significantly over time.  I can assess mean percent change in occupancy over time, but I'm not sure how to assess that change with respect to uncertainty associated with the predicted occupancy values.  My feeling is that some kind of simulation testing needs to be performed, but I'm not sure how to do that.  Any suggestions would be much appreciated.  Thanks.
Best,
--N

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] testing for significant differences in species distribution predictions
parts:
Dear Neil,

depends on what you mean by 'testing whether occupancy changes'. The simplest would be the total area occupied, but more complex would be to test for differences in spatial patterns of occupancy. For the former, you could estimate the total number of occupied sites in your study area for each of the three periods by summing up the empirical Bayes estimates of the latent occupancy state over all sites. To gauge the uncertainty in each of these, you could do a nonparametric bootstrap for 100 or 1000 times (depends on how long this takes for your data set). That is, each time, you take (with replacement) a sample of sites of the same size as your original data set, fit the model, do the predictions and get the number of occupied sites and save that. I guess from the bootstrap samples of the area occupied for each of the three periods you could make some 'significance statement'.

If you are interested in spatial patterns of occupancy, then I would go into the species distribution modeling literature and see what they do. I believe I have seen a kappa statistics or something used for expressing the difference between two spatial patterns (nor sure though). Perhaps, to say something about the significance of such a statistic, you could use the nonpar bootstrap as well.

Regards  --  Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] testing for significant differences in species distribution predictions
parts:
Dear Neil,

not sure I understand what you mean by "latent abundance ... not the actual abundance, but an abundance index ...". I mean you use the Nmix model to get at an estimate of the actual abundance. Unless your model is quite wrong, and ignoring the issue of not knowing your effective sample area (cf. spatial caprecap), the Nnmix should give you an estimate of actual abundance.

But apart from that, yes, you can do the same as for occurrence, i.e., you can get the empirical Bayes estimate of the latent abundance at each pixel and then sum that up over the entire domain. Doing this many times with a nonparametric bootstrap sample of your data will give you some measure of the uncertainty around this estimate and you can use that to say whether this total hs changed from one point in time to another.

Actually, it occurs to me now that this, and what I said in my earlier email, is not quite correct: you can get the empirical Bayes estimates of the latent occurrence or abundance states only for sites where you have observed detection/nondetection ("presence/absence") or count data, but not for those sites where you only have the environmental covariate values, but not the "response". So what you do is to sum up (over all pixels) the *predictions* of occupancy probability (in the site-occ model) or of lambda (in the Nmix).

Kind regards  --  Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] testing for significant differences in species distribution predictions
parts:
Dear Marc,
Thanks for your patience and help in on this topic. I should clarify some. In addition to occupancy modeling, I want to evaluate and map tiger habitat selection.  I used the Nmix model to evaluate the effects of land-cover composition and spatial configuration (using landscape metrics)  on tiger abundance at 76 sites, and then based on the coefficients, predicted tiger "abundance" across a grid with a resolution equal to that of the remotely sensed image (30 x 30 m) from which the covariates were derived from.  I used the results from the same best-fit model to predict "abundances" for two time periods in the past.  I don't think the per grid cell predictions can be meaningfully interpreted as true tiger abundances, per se, because the grid cells are far smaller than a tiger's home range.  Nevertheless, based on the assumption that more tigers will select a location if it is better habitat, I think the per-cell index of abundance can be an appropriate proxy for habitat selection. 
I have summed up the predictions across all of the pixels over the three time periods as you suggest.  There are differences, but I'm still not sure if they are meaningfully large differences.  It seems like repeatedly drawing from some underlying distribution of the coefficients and then simulating the predictions across space a number of times to generate a simulation mean and CIs would be a way to go.  Would this adequately address my question?  If so, is the option currently available in unmarked? 
Thanks again.

--Neil
